samples.summary: CLI consent interstitial is framable — no X-Frame-Options / CSP frame-ancestors anywhere in the backend, so the new "human confirmation" binding is clickjackable from any same-site page
samples.evidence: `githubAuth` renders the new consent page with `res.type('html').send(...)` (auth.controller.ts:122-127) and no framing headers. I grepped the whole `packages/` tree for `helmet|X-Frame-Options|frame-ancestors|Content-Security-Policy|frameguard` and the only hit is a spell dictionary — the app sets none globally either (packages/backend/src/main.ts has no helmet). This page is documented as the *last* line of defence for the CLI flow: the guard's own comment (github-auth.guard.ts:217-224) says the nonce, the PKCE challenge and the browser-binding cookie are all held by whoever *wrote* the start URL, so only the deliberate click on this page stops `…/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<attacker's listener>&nonce=…&code_challenge=…`. Attack: attacker frames `https://api.example.com/auth/github?mode=cli&port=…` and UI-redresses the `<a class="continue">` link so the victim clicks it; the login proceeds to GitHub and the victim's code is delivered to the attacker's loopback listener. Mitigation that partially holds: `wafflebase_cli_confirm` is `SameSite=Lax`, so in a *cross-site* iframe it is not sent on the framed click and the gate re-renders. But `SameSite` is eTLD+1-based, and this deployment explicitly assumes frontend and backend share eTLD+1 (auth.controller.ts:468 comment), so any same-site page — the frontend itself, a sibling subdomain, an HTML injection on either — is same-site, the Lax cookie *is* sent, and the clickjack succeeds. `__Host-` does not prevent framing. Fix: send `X-Frame-Options: DENY` (or `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'`) on this response, and preferably require a POST for the continue action.

samples.summary: `bindingSecret` reuses `JWT_SECRET` as the HMAC key for OAuth state binding — cryptographic key reuse across two unrelated purposes
samples.evidence: `bindingSecret()` returns `configService.get('JWT_SECRET')` and `stateSignature()` HMACs the state-cookie value with it (github-auth.guard.ts:129-151). The same secret signs session/refresh JWTs (auth.module.ts:19, HS256 = HMAC-SHA256). I could not build a concrete forgery — the signed message is a server-generated random base64url value, never an attacker-chosen `header.payload` — so this is hardening, not an exploit. But an unauthenticated `GET /auth/github` now emits an HMAC-SHA256 tag under the JWT signing key on every request, which is exactly the property key separation exists to avoid. Derive a distinct key (e.g. `HKDF(JWT_SECRET, 'oauth-state')`) instead.

samples.summary: `GET /auth/github` is unauthenticated and unconditionally overwrites the single-slot `wafflebase_oauth_state` cookie, so any cross-site page can break a victim's in-flight browser login
samples.evidence: Every request to `/auth/github` calls `issueLoginCookie(context, OAUTH_STATE_COOKIE)` (github-auth.guard.ts:301-307), which `res.cookie(...)` overwrites the browser's only state slot. An attacker page can emit `` (or an iframe); the cross-site response's `Set-Cookie` for a `SameSite=Lax` cookie is still stored, replacing the value the victim's genuine in-flight login was bound to. When GitHub redirects the victim back, `verifyCallbackState` recomputes the HMAC of the *new* cookie, the compare fails, and the victim is bounced to `/login?error=login_state`. This is a login-availability issue only (no session is issued to the attacker) and it also affects two honest concurrent tabs, but the change went to explicit lengths to give CLI and browser flows separate cookie names for exactly this collision (github-auth.guard.ts:19-31) and left the browser-vs-browser / attacker-triggered case single-slot. A per-login cookie name suffix or a small list of accepted values would close it.

samples.summary: `nonce` is length-bounded but not charset-restricted, unlike `code_challenge`, and is stored and echoed into the loopback redirect
samples.evidence: `boundedToken(req.query?.nonce, 1, MAX_NONCE_LENGTH)` (github-auth.guard.ts:261) passes no `pattern`, while the challenge on line 266-271 is restricted to `/^[A-Za-z0-9\-._~]+$/`. So up to 128 arbitrary characters are stored and later reflected into `Location: http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?...&state=<nonce>` (auth.controller.ts:239) and into the consent page's link (auth.controller.ts:149). I traced both sinks: the redirect uses `encodeURIComponent` and the page uses `URLSearchParams` + `escapeHtml`, so I could not build an injection — no CRLF, no HTML break-out. Reported as defence-in-depth: the value is attacker-influenceable and reflected into a redirect URL, and a future sink that forgets to encode would be an injection. Applying the same base64url pattern to the nonce costs nothing (the CLI already sends base64url).

samples.summary: `login-url.txt` is written after an unlinking `rmSync`, a symlink-follow window in whatever directory `WAFFLEBASE_CONFIG` points at
samples.evidence: `announceLoginUrl` does `rmSync(file, {force:true})` then `writeFileSync(file, url, {mode: 0o600})` (login.ts:226-227). Between the two calls a local user who can create entries in `dirname(getConfigPath())` can plant a symlink; `writeFileSync` with the default `'w'` flag follows it, writing this login's nonce and PKCE challenge to a file of their choosing (and `mode` would not apply to the pre-existing target). The default path is `~/.wafflebase/` (user-owned, 0755 by `mkdirSync`), so this is not exploitable in the normal case — but `WAFFLEBASE_CONFIG` can point anywhere, including a shared `/tmp` as the repo's own tests do. `writeFileSync(file, url, {mode: 0o600, flag: 'wx'})` without the preceding `rmSync` closes it.

samples.summary: `ERROR_MESSAGES[error]` is an unguarded prototype-chain lookup on an attacker-supplied query value
samples.evidence: `error` comes straight from `useSearchParams().get("error")` (login-form.tsx:28) and indexes a plain object literal (line 13). `?error=constructor`, `?error=toString`, `?error=valueOf` resolve on `Object.prototype`, return a truthy function, so `?? FALLBACK_ERROR` does not fire and a function is rendered as a React child. Impact is limited to a broken/warning render of the login page from a crafted link (no script execution — React escapes and refuses function children), but the login page is the one place this change routes failed OAuth callbacks to. Use `Object.hasOwn(ERROR_MESSAGES, error)` or a `Map`.

samples.summary: CLI consent page carries a single-use credential in its markup but sets no `Cache-Control: no-store`
samples.evidence: The rendered page embeds `cli_confirm=<confirmToken>` in the continue link (auth.controller.ts:151-153) and the same response sets that token as a cookie, yet `res.type('html').send(...)` (line 122) adds no cache directives — Express will attach an ETag and no `Cache-Control`. The CLI's own equivalent redirect does set `'Cache-Control': 'no-store'` (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:379), so the asymmetry looks unintended. Shared caches generally decline to store `Set-Cookie` responses, which is why this is a nit rather than a leak I can demonstrate; adding `no-store, private` on the response removes the question.

verdict.reason: The absence claim checks out. The CLI consent interstitial is sent as bare HTML with no framing headers (auth.controller.ts:121-127, HTML body 156-188 has no CSP meta), and nothing sets X-Frame-Options or CSP frame-ancestors anywhere: main.ts:30-79 registers only body-parser/cookie-parser/ValidationPipe/CORS (no helmet, no header middleware), a repo-wide grep for helmet|X-Frame-Options|frame-ancestors|Content-Security-Policy|frameguard|add_header outside node_modules hits only docs prose (docs/design/homepage.md:291) and a spell dictionary, and every backend setHeader call site sets only Content-Type/Disposition/Cache-Control/X-Content-Type-Options (files.controller.ts:153-156, document-file.controller.ts:61-64, image.controller.ts:71-75, miro.controller.ts:82-88). There is also no edge proxy in-repo (docker-compose.yaml has no nginx/traefik/caddy, no ingress or nginx conf) that could add it. The gate being protected is genuinely the last line of defence: github-auth.guard.ts:279-288 renders this page instead of redirecting to GitHub, and hasConfirmation (313-325) is satisfied by a GET query param echoing a SameSite=Lax, Path=/ cookie (loginCookieOptions 104-111). Lax cookies ARE sent on same-site subframe navigations, and the deployment assumes frontend+backend share eTLD+1 (auth.controller.ts:468), so a same-site framing page can UI-redress the plain <a class="continue"> link (line 185) and drive the victim through GitHub to an attacker-chosen loopback port (callback redirect at auth.controller.ts:240-242). __Host- constrains cookie writing, not framing. In-lane for the security rubric (bypass of an auth confirmation gate) and correctly rated major: exploitation requires an attacker-controlled same-site page, so it is a clear weakness rather than a standalone full exploit.

finding.summary: HMAC-"signed" double submit adds no defence against the cookie-planting attacker it is documented to stop; outside NODE_ENV=production the forced-login CSRF (and the CLI browser-binding) is still fully open
finding.evidence:
`stateSignature()` (github-auth.guard.ts:108) computes `state = w.HMAC(JWT_SECRET, cookieValue)` and the comment at lines 100-107 claims "the attacker can plant a cookie but cannot produce the `state` that matches it, so the forced-login CSRF stays shut even where the prefix cannot be used" (repeated in docs/design/backend.md and rest-api.md).

That is false. The cookie value is server-generated and returned to the requester: a single unauthenticated `curl -i https://backend/auth/github` yields both halves of a *valid* pair — `Set-Cookie: wafflebase_oauth_state=C` and `Location: https://github.com/...&state=w.HMAC(C)` (guard lines 249-255 mint both on the same response). An attacker who can plant a cookie for the registrable domain therefore plants exactly that `C` and replays the matching signature; the HMAC buys nothing over a plain double submit. The only control that actually resists cookie planting is the `__Host-` prefix, and `secureCookies()` (line 44-46) turns it off — along with `Secure` — for every deployment that does not set `NODE_ENV=production` (self-hosted docker/compose behind TLS is the common case). In such a deployment a sibling-subdomain XSS/takeover or an http `Set-Cookie` injection re-opens the forced-login CSRF this change exists to close.

The CLI half is weaker still: `StateEntry.browserBinding` is stored and compared as the raw cookie value (auth.controller.ts:294-299), so the same cookie planter — who mints the CLI state token themselves and so already knows it — completes the CLI forced-login and captures an authorization code for the victim's account at their own loopback port, which the risk table in docs/design/rest-api.md asserts is prevented.

A state that is bound to something the attacker cannot obtain (e.g. HMAC over cookie value *plus* a per-login server secret the attacker never receives, or a server-side entry keyed by the cookie) is what the comment describes; this implementation is not it. At minimum the security claim in the

verdict.reason: The code is not as described. (a) The comment the finding quotes as falsely claiming "the attacker can plant a cookie but cannot produce the state" does not exist; stateSignature's doc comment (github-auth.guard.ts:133-148) explicitly states the opposite — "What it does not buy... protection against an attacker who can plant cookies... one request hands the caller a matching pair... Cookie planting is closed by __Host- and by nothing else here" — and the same caveat is repeated at the class comment (lines 196-200) and at the callback verifier (auth.controller.ts:277-279). (b) secureCookies() is at lines 71-75, not 44-46, and is NOT gated only on NODE_ENV=production: it also returns true whenever the configured GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL is https (line 73-74), with the rationale at lines 60-69 explicitly citing "a staging box, a self-hosted install, a container image whose entrypoint forgot it". So the finding's exploit scenario (self-hosted docker behind TLS without NODE_ENV=production) receives Secure + __Host- via loginCookieName (lines 92-97); only a plain-http origin lacks it, which the code documents as an accepted limit (lines 87-90). (c) The docs allegedly repeating the false claim in fact state the corrected one: backend.md:110-114, backend.md:366-375, rest-api.md:413. The CLI risk row (rest-api.md:412) claims only browser-binding via the wafflebase_cli_state cookie plus the consent interstitial, not cookie-planting resistance. The finding's requested remediation ("at minimum correct the security claim") is already implemented in code comments and both design docs; its cited line numbers match no current code, indicating it describes a prior revision.

searchedFor: grep req.url|originalUrl across packages/backend/src for other URL log sites
finding.summary: New access-log redaction misses the share-link credential when it rides in the path: `GET /share-links/:token/resolve` is logged verbatim
finding.evidence:
`logSafeUrl` only ever touches the query string — `const query = url.indexOf('?'); if (query === -1) return url;` (log-safe-url.ts:102-103) — and `SENSITIVE_PARAMS` is keyed on parameter *names*. The share-link token is documented (and treated in this diff) as "the whole of that document's access control", and it is carried in two shapes:
- `GET /documents/:id/file?token=<t>` (document-file.controller.ts:40) — covered by the new `token` entry;
- `GET /share-links/:token/resolve` (share-link.controller.ts:67-68, unauthenticated, resolves documentId/role/title for the bearer) — the same credential as a *path segment*, which `logSafeUrl` returns untouched.

So the live token lands in the access-log `url` field in full. `customLogLevel` (app.module.ts:49-61) puts any 4xx/5xx on that route at `warn`/`error`, so it survives the default `info` level (and every request survives when `LOG_LEVEL=debug`, which is normal in staging) — exactly the "replayable credential parked in a file operators, log shippers and agent harnesses all read" that the new control was added to prevent. The redaction reads as covering the share credential (its own doc comment names it) while covering only one of its two carriers.

Searched: grep for `@Query('...')`/`@Param(` across packages/backend/src to enumerate credential-bearing routes; read share-link.controller.ts and document-file.controller.ts; read log-safe-url.ts and its spec — no path-segment redaction exists anywhere.

verdict.reason: The finding claims no path-segment redaction exists and that `logSafeUrl` early-returns any URL without a query string. Both are false in this repository. `log-safe-url.ts:75-79` defines `SECRET_PATH_SEGMENTS` with the rule `{ shape: ['share-links','*','resolve'], index: 1 }`, and `redactPathSecrets()` (lines 82-106) replaces that credential segment with `<redacted>` after decoding, lowercasing and collapsing empty segments. `logSafeUrl` line 153-154 does not return early: it only splits path from query, then line 159 runs `redactPathSecrets(rawPath)` on every non-/auth request and uses the result in both the no-query return (line 160) and the with-query return (line 163). The rule matches the real route: `share-link.controller.ts:22` is `@Controller()` (no prefix) and `:67` is `@Get('share-links/:token/resolve')`, and `setGlobalPrefix` has zero matches in packages/backend/src, so the logged URL is exactly `/share-links/<token>/resolve` — three segments, matching the shape check at lines 95-97. Behavior is covered by tests at log-safe-url.spec.ts:73-92 (including case-variant, doubled-slash, trailing-slash and query-string spellings) and scoped narrowly at :97-105. The share token is therefore redacted in the access log for this route, so the alleged exposure does not occur.
